explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Abraham had six sons by Keturah and still, "Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac." Everything. That's the whole bakery going to one stamper. And notice he didn't leave the other sons empty-handed either, as we'll see in a moment (Genesis 25:5-6).

I can see why you'd say that, friend. With six more sons running around, you'd think the inheritance got sliced up like a big sheet of cookie dough. But the text says, "Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac." Everything, not just a piece of it (Genesis 25:5).

That's it, baker. "Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines" while he was still alive, and then he sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east (Genesis 25:6). So they left with something in their hands. The text doesn't say what the gifts were, so I won't guess.

Nice thinking, friend, but the text never mentions land for them. It says Abraham gave them gifts and sent them to the land of the east (Genesis 25:6). Now, that's a place they went, not a plot he handed over. The word is gifts, and that's all the verse tells us.

Ooh, that's a creative one, friend. But no servants are mentioned in this verse. What it says is that Abraham "gave gifts to the sons of his concubines" and sent them away to the land of the east (Genesis 25:6). If there was a whole traveling crew, the text isn't telling us.

Right on, baker. Genesis 25:8 says Abraham "breathed his last and died, old and contented." Contented, friend. After 175 years, that's a man who is at peace. I'd bake a whole batch for that kind of ending.
I get it, friend, because a long life has plenty of rough spots. But the text says he died "old and contented" (Genesis 25:8). Contented, not troubled. That's how this chapter describes his goodbye.

Oh, I can picture it, friend. A man of 175 tossing and turning like me on a hot day in the drawer. But that's not what the verse says. It says Abraham died "old and contented" (Genesis 25:8). Calm and settled, not restless.

That's right, baker. "Abraham was buried there with his wife Sarah" (Genesis 25:10). The cave of Machpelah was in the field he bought from the Hittites, so the two of them rest in the same place. I think there's something tender about that.

Good guess, friend, since Terah, Abraham's father, is part of his family story. But this passage says Abraham was buried "with his wife Sarah" (Genesis 25:10). Terah isn't named there. The text puts Abraham beside Sarah.

Nahor is Abraham's brother, so I see why he popped into your head, friend. But he's not the one in this verse. The text says Abraham was buried in the field he bought from the Hittites "with his wife Sarah" (Genesis 25:10).
Yes, baker! "After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac" (Genesis 25:11). Abraham was gone, but God's blessing kept moving. Isaac lived near Beer-lahai-roi when it happened.

Close to a real moment, friend, because God did test Abraham earlier, when He told him to offer up Isaac (Genesis 22:1). But this verse is different. It says God "blessed" Isaac after Abraham died (Genesis 25:11). Blessing, not testing, this time.

I see why that word came to mind, friend, since God called Abraham to leave his home in the first place (Genesis 12:1). But in this verse, the word is "blessed." After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac (Genesis 25:11).

You got it, baker. Hagar the Egyptian was Sarah's maidservant, and she bore Ishmael to Abraham (Genesis 25:12). The text names her by her place in the household, so I'll do the same. Ishmael has his own account right here.

Keturah is a real name from this chapter, friend, so that's a fair pick. She's the wife who bore Abraham six sons (Genesis 25:1-2). But Ishmael's mother is a different woman. The verse says "Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant" (Genesis 25:12).

Milcah is a name from Abraham's family, friend. She was the wife of his brother Nahor (Genesis 11:29). She isn't Ishmael's mother, though. The verse says he was born to "Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant" (Genesis 25:12).

I'd love that to be the answer, friend, but the text says something else. The last line of the passage says Ishmael's descendants "lived in hostility toward all their brothers" (Genesis 25:18). So this one is false. Hostility, not peace.

That's right, baker. Genesis 25:18 says Ishmael's descendants "lived in hostility toward all their brothers." Not peace, hostility. That's a hard note to end on, and the text doesn't say more about why. This closes out Abraham's story, and the story of God's promises keeps going.
